clinicalPearls: A diagnosis of exclusion: renal failure in advanced cirrhosis/portal hypertension (with or without ascites) that fails to improve after volume expansion and stopping diuretics
Kidneys are structurally normal — HRS is a functional, potentially reversible form of renal hypoperfusion driven by splanchnic vasodilation and effective arterial underfilling
Newer nomenclature classifies HRS as HRS-AKI (rapidly progressive, formerly type 1) versus HRS-NAKI (slower, chronic course, formerly type 2)
Urinalysis and urine sediment are typically bland, with minimal proteinuria and few cells or casts
Urine sodium is usually very low, reflecting intense renal sodium avidity from neurohormonal activation
A common precipitant is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or other infection, so sepsis must always be actively sought and excluded
Trial of volume expansion (typically with albumin) for 48 hours with cessation of diuretics/nephrotoxins is required before the diagnosis can be confirmed
Definitive treatment is liver transplantation; medical therapy is a bridge, not a cure
reference.pathophysiology: Advanced liver disease with portal hypertension causes marked splanchnic arterial vasodilation, which reduces effective circulating arterial volume despite total-body volume overload. This triggers compensatory activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system, and vasopressin release, producing intense renal vasoconstriction and a progressive fall in glomerular filtration despite normal renal histology. Systemic inflammation and bacterial translocation from the gut further worsen splanchnic vasodilation and renal hypoperfusion, and superimposed infection frequently precipitates the acute form.
additionalDifferentials: Prerenal azotemia from volume depletion (vomiting, diarrhea, over-diuresis, GI bleeding)
Acute tubular necrosis from ischemia, sepsis, or nephrotoxin exposure
Drug-induced acute kidney injury (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast, ACE inhibitors/ARBs)
Glomerulonephritis associated with chronic liver disease (e.g., IgA nephropathy, membranoproliferative pattern in hepatitis C)
Abdominal compartment syndrome from tense ascites
infectionMimics: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with secondary renal hypoperfusion
Urinary tract infection with associated prerenal physiology
nonInfectiousMimics: Prerenal azotemia from diuretic overuse or GI losses
Cardiorenal syndrome from cirrhotic cardiomyopathy or coexistent heart failure
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatinine trend and estimated GFR — establishes rate and severity of renal decline defining HRS-AKI vs HRS-NAKI
Urinalysis with microscopy — bland sediment supports HRS over intrinsic renal disease
Urine sodium and fractional excretion of sodium — typically very low, reflecting avid sodium retention
Renal ultrasound — excludes obstruction and assesses for underlying structural kidney disease
Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid cell count and culture — excludes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis as a precipitant
Blood and urine cultures — identify occult infection precipitating renal decline
Response to albumin volume challenge with diuretic withdrawal — required to confirm the diagnosis
Liver function panel and coagulation studies — assess severity of underlying hepatic decompensation and transplant urgency
redFlags: Rapidly rising creatinine meeting acute kidney injury criteria in a cirrhotic patient (HRS-AKI)
Concurrent signs of sepsis or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis requiring urgent source control
Oliguria or anuria with worsening encephalopathy or hemodynamic instability
Failure to respond to albumin challenge and vasoconstrictor therapy, indicating need for urgent transplant evaluation
Coexistent gastrointestinal bleeding masking or worsening true volume depletion
Multiorgan involvement suggesting acute-on-chronic liver failure
pitfalls: Diagnosing HRS before adequately excluding hypovolemia and completing an albumin challenge with diuretic withdrawal
Overlooking an occult infection (especially spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) as the precipitating trigger
Assuming a bland urinalysis excludes intrinsic renal disease entirely without considering overlap syndromes
Delaying nephrology and hepatology/transplant referral while pursuing prolonged medical trials in a rapidly deteriorating patient
reference.prognosis: Historically associated with very high short-term mortality, particularly the rapidly progressive form, unless renal function improves with therapy or the patient undergoes timely liver transplantation. Even with treatment response, underlying hepatic decompensation continues to drive long-term outcomes.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Cirrhosis and Its Complications; Acute Kidney Injury
management: Give a vasoconstrictor — terlipressin or noradrenaline — together with intravenous albumin to counter splanchnic vasodilation and restore effective arterial volume
Withdraw diuretics, non-selective beta-blockers, and nephrotoxins, and expand volume with albumin as both diagnostic challenge and treatment
Actively seek and treat precipitants, giving antibiotics for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or other infection and albumin to prevent renal injury in peritonitis
Use renal replacement therapy as a bridge in those awaiting transplantation or with a reversible precipitant
Prioritise liver transplantation as the definitive treatment, since the renal dysfunction is functional and often reversible once liver function is restored
Consider a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt in selected patients to reduce portal pressure
Monitor renal function, urine output, and for infection, escalating to intensive care for the rapidly progressive form

algorithms.title: ICA-HRS Diagnostic Criteria and Management Pathway (EASL/AASLD 2023)

steps.action: Patient with cirrhosis and ascites presenting with AKI: serum creatinine increase >= 0.3 mg/dL within 48h OR >= 50% increase from baseline.

Immediately stop all diuretics (spironolactone, furosemide), withhold vasodilators/beta-blockers, and discontinue all potential nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides). Treat underlying infection/SBP aggressively.
Administer IV Albumin 1 g/kg/day (maximum 100 g/day) for 48 hours. Assess response.
Absence of shock, no current/recent nephrotoxic drug exposure, absence of structural kidney disease (proteinuria < 500 mg/day, microhematuria < 50 RBC/HPF, normal renal ultrasound).

Initiate IV Terlipressin (continuous infusion 2 to 4 mg/day, titrate up to 12 mg/day) PLUS IV Albumin 20 to 40 g/day. Alternative if terlipressin unavailable: IV Noradrenaline infusion in ICU or Midodrine + Octreotide. Definite cure is liver transplantation.

tables.title: Differentiation of Renal Failure Phenotypes in Advanced Cirrhosis
rows: Pre-renal Azotemia
FENa < 0.2% (avid sodium retention)
Bland sediment; no protein
Rapid improvement; creatinine returns to baseline
Volume expansion with isotonic fluids or albumin; treat fluid losses
HRS-AKI (Hepatorenal Syndrome AKI)
FENa < 0.2% (extreme renal vasoconstriction)
Bland sediment; minimal or no proteinuria (< 500 mg/day)
No response after 48h volume expansion with albumin
Terlipressin + IV Albumin; evaluation for emergency liver transplantation
Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)
FENa > 1% to 2% (tubular epithelial dysfunction)
Muddy brown granular casts, tubular epithelial cells, proteinuria
No improvement; slow tubular recovery over 1 to 3 weeks
Supportive hemodialysis / CRRT; treat shock and sepsis; avoid fluid overload
Glomerulonephritis (e.g. IgA, Cryoglobulinemic)
Variable FENa
Dysmorphic red cells, RBC casts, significant proteinuria (> 1 g/day)
No response to volume expansion
Nephrology consultation; renal biopsy; disease-specific immunosuppression
tables.caption: Early differentiation between HRS-AKI and ATN is critical because vasoconstrictor response declines with prolonged ischemia.
